title: A gynecology appointment: preparation and consent
intro: Gynecology care can address bleeding, pelvic pain, contraception, pregnancy concerns or screening. A first visit does not automatically require an internal examination. You can ask what each part is for and decline or stop it.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Prepare your main questions, period pattern, symptoms, medicines and any possibility of pregnancy. You do not need to shave or use vaginal cleansing products before an appointment.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: The clinician explains proposed examinations and samples, checks consent and offers appropriate privacy. Request a chaperone, interpreter or preferred clinician where available; discuss pain or previous traumatic experiences only as much as you choose. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Tests and treatments depend on the concern. Cervical screening is different from investigation of symptoms; a recent normal screening result does not replace assessment of new bleeding or pain. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Ask about costs, confidentiality, how results will arrive and who to contact if nothing is received. For an intimate examination you may request a pause, smaller equipment or another appointment to discuss options. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Severe pelvic pain, fainting, heavy bleeding or pain with possible pregnancy require urgent assessment. Persistent bleeding after sex or after menopause needs prompt review rather than waiting for routine screening.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira attends for contraception and asks whether an internal examination would change the advice. The clinician explains the options and respects her decision.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben helps a partner write questions before the visit. She chooses whether he enters the room and can speak with the clinician privately.

questions: What findings support the diagnosis or recommendation?
What are the benefits, risks and alternatives for me?
When should I seek help or arrange a review?
